Waltz (Finale)
E♭ major

Movement IV · Waltz (Finale) · E♭ major

1095quarter-note beats85phrases365bars
123456789T

This finale is a sonata-rondo in waltz dress. Waltz A (mm.15–62) is followed by the trio complex in B♭ (mm.63–133), made up of the descent of rehearsal 60, the cantilena and the trio melody. Waltz A returns in E major (m.148) and, after an episode in C♭ major, is recapitulated at m.218. Because the trio complex also returns to the home key from m.249, transposed a fourth up and a fifth down, I read this layout as sonata-like. The Grandioso and the coda (mm.303–365) close the movement.

The home key is E♭ major, yet only 25 of the 1095 beats begin on a root-position tonic triad without added notes. In the tonal-context column, E♭ major accounts for 563 beats (51%), B♭ major for 141 and chromatic passing motion for 157. Every entry of Waltz A in E♭ begins over B♭7/F, and the root-position tonic arrives two or three bars later. The return in E major begins over B7/F♯, the Grandioso over F9. The dominant note B♭ moves to E♭ at m.345, and after that no triad with B♭ as its root sounds. The final cadence moves from a D major triad up a semitone to E♭ (mm.360–361).

I see three points that matter in performance. First, Waltz A’s center of gravity lies in the bar where the delayed tonic arrives; beneath the trio melody, too, a root-position B♭ does not sound until m.122. Second, the seam at m.152, where E major slides back to E♭, is heard as a progression from the Neapolitan chord to the tonic. Third, m.218 calls for a balance between Violin II’s original melody and the descant a third above it. Analytically, the harmonic skeleton consists of the two augmented triads formed by the introduction’s dyads, the major-third cycle of dominant sevenths and the tritone pairs. Just as the first movement closed ♭II–I, this movement too ends without passing through the dominant.

1INT

mm.1–14

Introduction — from a chordless motto chain to the first chord, B♭7/F

Six sighs marked sf pass between the violins and the lower strings. Each figure is a dyad a third wide decorated by its lower semitone neighbors, with neither bass nor chord. The first chord is the pizzicato B♭7/F of m.9, and with it E♭ is suggested for the first time. The zigzag figure of mm.9–10 is followed by the rising motto (mm.11–14). Under poco riten. only the third G–B remains, and the introduction stops before the double bar.

INT1Paragraph 1 — the motto chain

Tonal contextNo tonic: third-related dyads without a bass

INT1a

The motto’s first three dyads

m.1, beat 1 to m.5, beat 1Tonally open (dyads without a bass)

E♭5/G5, F♯4/A4 and C♭4/E♭4 sound in turn in the violins, the lower strings and the violins again. Each takes the shape of the motto: the dyad falls to the dyad a semitone lower at beat 1& and returns. In m.2 the cello rises above the viola, a voice crossing. The third dyad is held to the end of m.4, where a break occurs. Only two notes sound at any moment, so neither a root nor a key is determined.

INT1b

Answer a minor third lower, halting on G–B

m.5, beat 1 to m.9, beat 1Tonally open; halts on G–B (implying the dominant of C minor)

The music of mm.5–6 is mm.1–2 transposed down a minor third, with the roles of the violins and the lower strings exchanged. The last dyad does not arrive on the C♭/E♭ of mm.3–4 lowered by a minor third, A♭/C, but a semitone below that, on G3/B3. Measured from mm.3–4, this lies a major third lower. The major thirds of mm.1, 3 and 7 belong to the augmented triad E♭–G–B, and their neighbor notes to the augmented triad B♭–D–F♯.

FINDING 1Waltz A’s melody leaps to the A♭/C that the introduction avoided
FINDING 1

Waltz A’s melody leaps to the A♭/C that the introduction avoided

The music of mm.5–7 lies a minor third below mm.1–3, except that its last dyad arrives not on A♭/C but a semitone lower, on G3/B3. A♭/C first appears at m.15, as A♭5/C6, the goal of Waltz A’s leap. When the rising motto reaches A♭5/C6 at m.147, Waltz A enters in E major.

INT2Paragraph 2 — the zigzag figure and the rising motto

Tonal contextFrom V7 of E♭ major to G–B, which suggests the dominant of C minor

INT2a

Pizzicato B♭7/F and the zigzag figure

m.9, beat 1 to m.11, beat 1From the dominant of E♭ major to a chromatic line

The movement’s first chord is the dominant of E♭ major, with its fifth, F, in the bass. Violin I alternates rising minor sevenths and falling tritones in eighth notes; only the last interval, E5→B4, is a perfect fourth. The minor-seventh pairs B♭–A♭, D–C and F♯–E are the shells of seventh chords whose roots rise by major thirds. In mm.60–61 and mm.134–135 these three pairs are harmonized as dominant seventh chords.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.9, beat 1) ↓

INT2b

The rising motto: by semitones to G–B

m.11, beat 1 to m.15, beat 1Chromatic; halts on G–B (implying the dominant of C minor)

The rising motto is a gesture that leaps from a single note to a held dyad. The leaps rise by semitones: B4→F5/A5, C5→F♯5/A♯5, C♯5→G5/B5. The lower note of each dyad lies a tritone above the single note, the upper note a minor seventh above it. The leap thus gathers the two intervals of the zigzag figure into a single gesture. Both times the introduction stops on G–B; this time it lies two octaves above mm.7–8.

2WA

mm.15–62

Waltz A — beginning over B♭7/F, with a new bass in the restatement that delays the tonic

Waltz A begins at rehearsal 54 over B♭7/F, and the tonic appears only at m.17. Phrase a closes with V9–I at m.22, and its answer a′ makes a half cadence on B♭ at m.30. After the motto interlude the same pair returns reharmonized. This time D♭ and the Neapolitan F♭ delay the tonic, and a′ also cadences on E♭, at m.51. The codetta (rehearsal 59), in which the zigzag figure and the motto return, ends on B♭7 at m.62.

3TRIO

mm.63–133

Trio complex — a chromatic descent opens B♭; the cantilena and the trio melody hold B♭

At rehearsal 60 the cello sinks chromatically beneath planed chords and reaches the German sixth of B♭ major at m.74. B♭ major is established by the cello’s cantilena and the trio melody. The stringendo sequence reaches C♭ major, the ♭II, and ii9–V13 follows. At rehearsal 64 the descent of rehearsal 60 returns a fourth lower, a minor third lower and at its original pitch. At m.133 it is cut off by a French-sixth sonority.

TRIO1Paragraph 1 — chromatic descent and planing (rehearsal 60)

Tonal contextFrom E♭ major through planed chords to the German sixth of B♭ major

TRIO1a

Major triads planed by semitones

m.63, beat 1 to m.67, beat 1From E♭ major to chromatic planing

At rehearsal 60 (Poco più mosso, dotted half = 92) B♭7 resolves to E♭. The cello at once begins to sink by semitones in syncopation. Pizzicato and col legno, the upper three parts plane major triads from E♭ to A. When the bass lies a semitone below the triad, the result is a maj7 chord in third inversion; when it lies a whole step below, a dominant seventh in third inversion. The cello reaches A♭2 at m.66 beat 3 and rises B♭2–C3–D3 to link to the next stage.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.63, beat 1) ↓

TRIO1b

A chain of half-diminished sevenths and whole-tone sonorities

m.67, beat 1 to m.71, beat 1Chromatic (planing)

The bass line is mm.63–66 moved up a semitone. The upper three parts play the root, fifth and seventh of half-diminished seventh chords, and the cello supplies the third. This shape descends by semitones from C♯ø7/E to A♭ø7/C♭. Each time the bass moves down early, on the off-beat, a whole-tone sonority (an augmented triad with an added seventh) is inserted. In m.70 the bass stays on the major third, and French-sixth-type sonorities follow one another: G7♭5, G♭7♭5, F7♭5.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.67, beat 1) ↓

TRIO1c

Shrinking units, then the German sixth

m.71, beat 1 to m.75, beat 1From chromatic planing to the German sixth of B♭ major

In all four parts, m.71 and m.73 transpose m.67 up a major second and a major third respectively. In m.72 the bass stays on E3, and on beat 3 the upper voices return to the C♯ø7/E of m.67 beat 2. The four-bar unit shrinks to two bars, and its starting bass rises by whole steps: E3, G♭3, A♭3. In m.74 the German sixth is complete on beat 3, over the held G♭3. It resolves to F at m.75, and the process of planing ends.

The introduction comes back to life at rehearsal 65. The zigzag figure is sequenced by semitones over dominant seventh chords that rise by major thirds. Because the rising motto continues to A♭–C, a semitone higher than in the introduction, Waltz A enters in E major. The phrase slides back to E♭ for its cadence (mm.152–155). The answer a′ ends on B♭, as at m.30. At rehearsal 68 the motto chain and the zigzag figure are compressed into brilliant passage-work over the dominant.

Recapitulation of the trio complex — settled in E♭ a fourth higher and a fifth lower; the V13 of B♭ becomes V9/V of E♭

The cello’s cantilena passes to both violins and returns note for note a perfect fourth higher (mm.249–262). The trio melody returns a perfect fifth lower, and in mm.264–289 the sonorities match beat for beat. The harmony changes in mm.290–295, where the model’s ii9 becomes V9/V. The dominant pedal on B♭ acquires a trill. At rehearsal 79 the descent of rehearsal 60 is compressed and leads through a diminished-seventh arpeggio into the Grandioso.

TRR1Paragraph 1 — the cantilena a fourth higher (rehearsal 76)

Tonal contextE♭ major (mm.75–88 a fourth higher), through ♭II to B♭7

First half of the cantilena and a Neapolitan color

m.249, beat 1 to m.257, beat 1E♭ major (at m.250 an F♭ = E major color)

At Poco più mosso (dotted half = 92) both violins begin the melody in unison. The B♭7/A♭ of m.248 resolves to I6 at m.249 beat 2. In m.250 the viola raises its figure a semitone, producing the sound of an E major triad (F♭, ♭II). This ♭II returns to the tonic at m.251 without passing through the dominant. In mm.252–255 chromatic notes are added, and through V7 the melody reaches E♭4 at m.256.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.249, beat 1) ↓

m.257, beat 1 to m.263, beat 3E♭ major: from prolonged I to V (B♭, colored by V/V)

The melody climbs from F4 and reaches B♭4. Beneath it the viola’s descending scales start higher bar by bar and arrive at B♭4 at m.261 beat 1. In mm.260–261 the F major triad (V/V) and the E♭ major triad alternate beneath the upper-voice B♭. In mm.262–263 I and V6 alternate every eighth note. The inner voices’ descent in thirds that follows leads to B♭7 (without its third), the pickup of the next phrase.

FINDING 10In the recapitulation the trio’s ♭II becomes E major, the key in which Waltz A returned
FINDING 10

In the recapitulation the trio’s ♭II becomes E major, the key in which Waltz A returned

The E major of mm.281–284 is the B major of mm.107–110 a fifth lower. It is the ♭II (F♭) of E♭ major, which was the Neapolitan chord at m.45 and the key of Waltz A at m.148. At m.250, too, the model’s B-minor-triad color is replaced by an E major triad.

On m.284 beat 3 E/B (F♭/C♭, I6/4) is complete, and the sequence reaches its farthest point on the sharp side. E7/B moves to the B♭7 of m.285 merely by the bass falling a semitone, and the two chords share the tritone D–G♯ (A♭).

The augmented sixth A♭–F♯ proceeds, with an A♭ major triad in between, to I6 at m.288. In m.289 the bass falls to G♭, and the music passes through vii°7/V to i6 (the E♭ minor triad/G♭).

8GRA

mm.303–334

Grandioso — Waltz A’s head turns into leaps, and a chain of German sixths climbs to ii9–V7

At rehearsal 80 the theme’s head becomes an octave leap. I read this passage as the apotheosis of Waltz A. The tail is compressed into eighth notes and closes on E♭ at m.310 beat 2. At rehearsal 81 the gesture of a′ rides on a rising bass, and the tail is repeated. Rehearsal 82 then retraces the bass of mm.244–247 and turns it into a chain of German sixths. Finally the music climbs through m.332, the bar in 2/4, to ii9–V7.

9CODA

mm.335–365

Coda — from a new figure over a B♭ pedal to a D → E♭ cadence without the dominant

Over the cello’s B♭ pedal a figure begins that continues the motto’s E♭–D–E♭ with a falling fourth. Once the dominant note B♭ has moved to E♭ at m.345, no triad with B♭ as its root sounds again. At rehearsal 84 the motto returns as parallel triads. At rehearsal 85 the dyads of mm.56–59 are recalled over C minor, F♯ minor and D major triads. After the D major triad resolves up a semitone to E♭, the movement ends on E♭ chords and a unison.

FINDING 12The final cadence D→E♭ is the waltz’s neighbor chord put in root position
FINDING 12

The final cadence D→E♭ is the waltz’s neighbor chord put in root position

The D→E♭ of mm.360–361 is a cadence that sets in root position the neighbor-chord motion D/A→E♭/B♭ heard since m.17. From m.345 on, the leading tone D never sounds as the third of the dominant. The only dominant is the thirdless B♭–F of mm.353–356.

Every beat

Beat-by-beat analysis

Choose a bar range or a phrase to read a short stretch. Open “Sounding notes and bass” to check each reading against the actual pitches of the four parts.

How to read the table (positions, chord labels, functions)
  • E♭ major is the global home key. The tonal context column names a local frame or implication, not a new modulation on every beat.
  • All beat numbers count quarter notes. The movement is in 3/4, with three beats in every bar; the exceptions are m.248 (2/2, four beats) and m.332 (2/4, two beats). There is no pickup: m.1 is the first full bar. Metronome marks are given in dotted half notes (one bar counted as one beat), a different unit from the beats of the text. The 2/2 of m.248 is an alla breve sign in the printed score.
  • An ampersand (&) marks the exact halfway point of a beat. +1/4 and +3/4 are the positions that divide the beat into four; +1/3 and +2/3 are the triplet positions that divide a quarter-note beat into three. Other fractions likewise mark the exact point within the beat where the sonority changes. In the text a position is written “beat 2 + 1/4”; in chord labels a change within the beat is written “+1/4”. In the label column of the beat table, & is written +1/2.
  • In a chord label, a chord written before the first semicolon (;) or arrow (→) normally sounds at the start of the beat. The offsets that follow are fractions of that same quarter-note beat. Where a label names an upper triad although the bass is moving, the triad is being prolonged; every actual change of the lowest note is shown in the sounding-note evidence.
  • The note name after a slash is the lowest sounding pitch, including where voices cross. no3 and no5 mean that the chord member does not sound. ø7 is a half-diminished seventh chord and °7 a diminished seventh chord. maj7 (a major seventh chord) is distinguished from the 7 of a dominant seventh. Added tones that sound together with the chord are kept in the label. Dyads also join their note names with a slash, but this is not the slash of a chord label: they are written lower note/upper note (for example E♭5/G5).
  • Roman numerals refer to the stated tonal context. In E♭: I = E♭, ii = F minor, iii = G minor, IV = A♭, V = B♭, vi = C minor, viiø7 = D–F–A♭–C. V/x and vii°7/x name an applied dominant or leading-tone chord of x. Inversions are written with figured-bass numbers, as in V6/4 or V4/2; V4/2/IV means the dominant seventh of IV in third inversion.
  • I read the form as A–B–A–C–A–B–A–coda. A is the waltz (m.15), B the trio complex (B♭, m.63) and C the episode (m.176). A returns at m.148 (E major), m.218 (recapitulation) and m.303 (Grandioso), and B returns in E♭ at m.249. The material tags in the beat table are as follows. M = the motto (the third dyad of m.1 with its lower semitone neighbors). M′ = the rising motto (m.11). T = the zigzag figure (the leaping figure of m.9). A = Waltz A (a = mm.15–22, a′ = mm.23–30, head = mm.15–18, tail = mm.19–22). B1 = the descent of rehearsal 60. B2 = the cello cantilena (m.75). B3 = the trio melody (m.90). C = the episode material (m.176). D = the coda figure (m.335).
  • Chord labels follow the spelling of the printed score (for example the D♯ major triad of m.150 and the C♯ of m.113). Keys are named by function, with the notated spelling added in parentheses (for example F♭ major (written as E major), C♭ major (written as B major)). Where the text writes “E major (F♭)”, it refers to the same region. The number after a note name is the octave number, with C4 as middle C (E♭2 is the E♭ above the cello’s lowest string). It is distinct from the numbers in chord symbols (B♭7, F9).
  • Paragraphs and phrases are analytical groupings based on entries, rests, cadences and thematic repetition. A phrase’s entry states whether it begins with an accompaniment prompt, a melodic pickup or a tied-over head. When a phrase span is given by its start and end positions, the end position itself is excluded (it coincides with the start of the next phrase). Bar ranges in the text (such as the Span lines) include both ends. Not every phrase ends in a cadence.
  • In the waltz accompaniment (a bass note on beat 1 and repeated chords on beats 2–3), the beat-1 bass and the chords of beats 2–3 are read together as one harmony. On a beat 1 where only the bass sounds, the label names only the notes actually sounding on that beat, and the function column supplies the relation to beats 2–3.
  • The beat table separates the literally sounding sonority from its harmonic function. Where there is no basis for a single functional root, sparse dyads and chromatic passing shapes are only described. Every subdivision within a beat can be checked in the sounding-note evidence, which appears in each beat’s “Sounding notes and bass at every change” panel in the interactive version and in the sounding_evidence column of the CSV.
  • The MuseScore transcription was made by optical recognition from a scan of the printed score and then corrected by checking all 365 bars against the scan. The notes in the sounding-note evidence are the notes of this transcription.
  • The confidence of each beat (high, medium, low) is kept in the JSON and the CSV. Where another reading is realistic, the text adds “can also be read as”; readings that rest on only two voices have medium confidence.

The cello's E♭2–B♭2–G3 and the viola's B♭3–G4–E♭5 strike the root-position tonic ff. Because the D-major triad moves up a semitone to the E♭-major triad, the cadence contains no dominant. The violins leap up from G4/B♭4 to E♭5/G5, and the D5/F♯5 of m.360 beat 3 resolves here.
